strengths: The paper introduces a novel and scientifically interesting problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from reading behavior, with both candidate selection and free-form reconstruction formulations.

The study uses a substantial public eye-tracking dataset spanning 180 information-seeking readers, 162 paragraphs, and 486 questions, and evaluates generalization to unseen readers, unseen texts, and their combination with article-level text separation.

The strongest result is meaningful: RoBERTEye-Fixations reaches 49.3% three-way accuracy versus approximately 33% chance, remains at 47.8% when both text and participant are unseen, and performs above chance when distinguishing questions sharing a critical span.

The comparison covers heuristic, recurrent, transformer, and generative models. The paper is generally clear, supplies extensive architectural and hyperparameter details, and explicitly discusses consent, demographic bias, and gaze-data privacy risks.
weaknesses: The central attribution to eye movements is insufficiently controlled. There is no text-and-question-only version of the strongest discriminative model, no shuffled-gaze control, and no ablation that destroys word-gaze alignment. The weak heuristic gaze baselines do not establish that the neural model's gain specifically reflects goal-conditioned scanpaths rather than dataset or assignment artifacts.

The baseline for the Different Spans diagnostic is misleading. Under Table 1's scoring, two-thirds of targets belong to span c2, so a majority-span predictor always choosing a c2 question obtains 66.7%, not the reported 55.5% random-choice figure. Haller RNN and both generative models fall below this elementary baseline, while RoBERTEye's 70.9% improvement over it is modest.

The evidence for open-ended reconstruction is weak. In the New Participant regime, the paragraph and its three exact target questions occurred in training, making reconstruction largely memorization plus selection. On genuinely new texts, DalEye-Llama has only 0.069 question-word kappa and 0.074 category kappa, and is worse than the same-span human baseline on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy. These results do not convincingly support the broad reconstruction claims.

The reconstruction metrics have limited validity. The QA metric gives an arbitrary GPT-4o question 66.7% accuracy on new texts, exceeding DalEye-Llama's 65.1%, demonstrating that it rewards passage/answer artifacts rather than faithful question recovery. It is also evaluated only on the 86% subset the QA model answers correctly, and no blinded human semantic evaluation is provided.

The uncertainty analysis is underspecified for the strongly crossed and repeated data. Across folds, most trials enter both New Text and New Participant evaluations; the reported mixed model lacks a trial-level or fold effect and is described as linear despite a binary outcome. The reconstruction bootstrap unit is unspecified despite repeated questions, texts, and participants. These choices can make confidence intervals and small significance claims anti-conservative.

The training description is internally inconsistent: Section 4 describes both generative models as next-token models trained on the correct question, whereas Appendix C.2 describes DalEye-LLaVA as contrastively optimized over the correct question and two distractors; the results section nevertheless states that the generative models were not explicitly trained for selection. This prevents a clear interpretation and faithful reproduction.

Technical novelty is limited because the successful system is primarily an adaptation of an existing encoder, while the two proposed generative systems are substantially weaker and DalEye-LLaVA is near chance. Reproducibility is further limited by the absence of released code, exact split assignments, random-seed variability, and decoding details.

The study is confined to one English news corpus, controlled reading, and a high-end eye tracker. Claims about real-time educational, accessibility, and web applications therefore substantially exceed the demonstrated setting, and the discussion could more fully address surveillance, secondary use, and sensitive-intent inference risks.

DalEye-Llama is worse than the same-span human distractor on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy, and its 65.1% QA score is below the 66.7% arbitrary GPT-4o baseline. The best selection model lacks indispensable no-gaze, shuffled-gaze, and gaze-feature ablations. Although labels are intended to be balanced, these controls are needed to demonstrate empirically that performance arises from participant-specific eye movements rather than textual features, question regularities, repeated-passage effects, or pipeline leakage, and to identify which gaze signals matter.

The reconstruction evaluation is not sufficiently reliable. There is no human assessment of semantic equivalence; BLEU and BERTScore reward lexical overlap; and the QA proxy often accepts unrelated questions, as demonstrated by high scores for arbitrary or incorrect questions. The statistical treatment needs clarification. Across the ten splits, most trials appear in both the new-text and new-participant regimes, yet aggregate tests do not explicitly model repeated predictions for the same trial or fold. The cognitive interpretation is partly circular: the analysis predicts model confidence using within- and outside-critical-span reading times, although the model directly consumes fixation-derived information aligned with the candidate question. These correlations show how the model responds to its inputs, not independent confirmation that it learned the proposed cognitive mechanism.

Model novelty is limited to adapting existing architectures and prompting or fine-tuning existing LLMs. Given that the task uses an existing dataset, acceptance would require especially decisive validation of the new formulation, which the reconstruction evaluation does not provide.

The very narrow confidence intervals and significance tests capture trial-level variation but not neural-training randomness; no repeated training seeds are reported. Aggregating overlapping cross-validation predictions also requires clearer handling of trial and fold dependence. Reproduction of the commercial GPT and preview Gemini results is further limited by missing decoding details and API dependence.

The applications discussion is premature given controlled laboratory hardware, a single English news domain, and modest accuracy. strengths: The paper introduces a novel and scientifically interesting problem, clearly separating candidate-based goal selection from candidate-free question reconstruction.
The underlying dataset is unusually substantial and well controlled for eye-tracking research, with 486 questions over 162 passages, repeated observations, and manually annotated critical spans.

Article-level splits evaluate unseen readers, unseen texts, and both simultaneously. The strongest selection result is meaningful: 49.3% versus 33.0% chance overall, including 47.8% on unseen texts and participants and 57.3% versus 49.9% for questions sharing a critical span.

The paper includes multiple architectures, human and text-only generation baselines, feature ablations, and cognitively motivated analyses. The presentation and appendix are generally clear and detailed.
The authors acknowledge consent, demographic bias, and some privacy concerns associated with eye tracking.
weaknesses: The central characterization as decoding arbitrary or open-ended goals is overstated. Every observed goal is one of exactly three experimenter-assigned questions per passage, rather than a spontaneous information need. In the new-participant reconstruction setting, the training data contain the same passage and exact target questions from other readers, reducing generation largely to memorization and implicit three-way selection.

The Gemini few-shot new-participant evaluation has severe target leakage. Its ten demonstrations come from the same paragraph but different participants, while only three questions are repeatedly assigned for that paragraph; the exact test question is therefore very likely to appear verbatim among the demonstrations. Moreover, there is no matched text-only few-shot control, so gains over arbitrary Gemini confound access to demonstrations with access to gaze.

The genuinely open-ended evidence on unseen texts is weak. For example, DalEye-Llama attains question-word accuracy of 0.545 versus 0.540 for its text-only counterpart and category accuracy of 0.450 versus 0.454. Its BLEU and BERTScore, 0.253 and 0.631, are below those of a deliberately incorrect human question sharing the critical span, 0.298 and 0.651. Improvements are small, inconsistent across models and metrics, and do not substantiate precise goal reconstruction.

The reconstruction metrics are inadequate for the headline claim. BLEU and BERTScore against one reference poorly assess question equivalence, the question-word and UIUC labels are very coarse, and the QA proxy can reward incorrect or vague questions—the incorrect same-span human baseline reaches 0.677 QA accuracy. No blinded human semantic evaluation or exact-recovery analysis is provided.

The selection baselines and ablations do not adequately isolate the source of the signal. Missing controls include a learned low-capacity critical-span model, shuffled or cross-participant scanpaths, average-gaze inputs, and an ablation that removes the fixation-to-word sequence itself. The full model scores 49.2%, while the purported linguistic-features-only variant scores 48.6% because it still retains gaze-derived fixation ordering; consequently, the added value of the extensive engineered gaze features is minimal and the mechanism remains unclear.

The statistical analysis raises concerns: linear mixed models are used for binary and bounded outcomes, predictions pooled across cross-validation models do not account for split or training-run variation, no question-level random effect is included, most families of comparisons lack multiplicity correction, and neural/API experiments have no multi-seed uncertainty analysis.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The displayed code link is blank, commercial and preview models limit repeatability, and important generation details such as decoding parameters, random seeds, few-shot sampling variability, and metric configurations are omitted.

External validity is narrow—native English-speaking adults, one news corpus, a controlled laboratory task, and a high-end EyeLink device. The proposed deployment in educational, media, and governmental interfaces is therefore premature, while risks involving covert inference of interests, profiling, data security, and mental privacy receive insufficient treatment.
